---
title: "Chapter 6: Fitting ecological response curves"
date: today
---

The exercises fit response curves to three data sets that the Chapter 5 practical used as a
backdrop for curves placed by eye: the titre of a virus in infected rabbits (Exercise 1),
the rate of an enzymatic reaction (Exercise 2) and the fecundity of fir trees (Exercise 3).
Exercise 4 simulates hypothetical samples from the model fitted in Exercise 1. Exercises 1
to 3 are the core of the practical and Exercise 4 is extra practice. Work through the
first exercise, which is worked in full on this page, before trying the remaining ones.
The ideas and notation are introduced in the [Chapter 6 theory](../Theory.qmd), and the
hints of each question point to the section that you need. Work through the exercises in
one R session: later exercises reuse the helper `cmb()` and the objects `critical_value`
and `n_sim` of Exercise 1.

As in the theory, every model is written and fitted with the packages RTMB and RTMBdist,
which you installed in the Chapter 1 practical together with `emdbook`, where the data of
Exercises 1 and 3 are. The scaled quantile residuals are calculated with the package
DHARMa, which you need to install once with `install.packages("DHARMa")`. Load RTMB first
and RTMBdist second:

```{r}
#| message: false
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)
```

# Exercise 1: Virus titre in infected rabbits

The data set `MyxoTiter_sum` in the package `emdbook` contains the titre of the myxoma
virus in the blood of European rabbits on different days after infection, for viruses of
four grades (Fenner and McIntyre 1956; the values were read from a figure in Dwyer et al.
1990). The titre measures the concentration of virus and is expressed as the logarithm in
base 10 of the number of rabbit infectious doses. As in the Chapter 5 practical, we keep
the 27 observations of grade 1, which were taken between 2 and 9 days after infection, and
put the day and the titre of each observation in a list of data:

```{r}
# Load the myxomatosis data from the emdbook package without attaching the package.
data(MyxoTiter_sum, package = "emdbook")

# Keep the observations of virus grade 1: the day after infection and the titre.
grade_1 = MyxoTiter_sum[MyxoTiter_sum$grade == 1, ]
titre_data = list(day = grade_1$day, titre = grade_1$titer)
```

In Exercise 1 of the [Chapter 5 practical](../../Chapter_5/Practicals/no_solution.qmd) we
described the rise and fall of the titre with the
[Ricker](../../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-ricker) function,
$f(x)=a\,x\,e^{-bx}$, where $x$ is the time since infection in days. From a peak read by
eye on day 6 with a titre of 7.6 we calculated $a=3.44$ units of titre/day and
$b=1/6\approx0.167$/day. Here we fit the curve to the observations, which we
treat as independent.

1. On paper, write the model with the Ricker curve for the mean titre and a
   [Normal](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-normal) observation model with a
   constant standard deviation $\sigma$. Give the units of $a$, $b$ and $\sigma$. The
   titres in these data are all positive; why can a Normal model, which allows any real
   value, be used for them?
2. Write the negative log-likelihood (NLL) with $\log(a)$, $\log(b)$ and $\log(\sigma)$ as
   parameters, and fit it from the values read by eye in the Chapter 5 practical. Check
   the convergence, report the estimates with their units, and draw the fitted curve over
   the data together with the curve by eye.
3. Calculate the standard errors and the correlation between the estimates with
   `sdreport()`. Ask for the time of the peak, $1/b$, and the height of the peak,
   $a/(be)$, on their original scale with `ADREPORT()`, and calculate 95% Wald intervals
   for both. Why can these intervals be calculated on the original scale here? Then calculate the
   likelihood profile interval of $b$ with `TMB::tmbprofile()` and `confint()`, and from
   it an interval for the time of the peak. Compare the two intervals for the time of the
   peak.
4. Simulate 1,000 hypothetical samples from the fitted model with `simulate()`, and
   calculate the scaled quantile residuals with DHARMa. Plot them, also against the day of
   the observation, and say what they show.
5. Fit the same curve with a [Gamma](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-gamma)
   observation model, with `dgamma()` and the arguments `shape` and `scale = mu / shape`.
   How does the spread of the titres around the curve differ between the two models?
   Compare them with AIC, AICc and BIC. Why do the three criteria give the same difference
   here?

## Solution

### Question 1

Let $Y_i$ be the titre of observation $i$ and $x_i$ the day after infection on which it
was measured. The curve describes the mean titre on each day, and the titres vary around
it according to a Normal distribution:

$$
Y_i \sim \operatorname{Normal}\left(f(x_i),\,\sigma^2\right),
\qquad
f(x)=a\,x\,e^{-bx},
\qquad i=1,\ldots,27,
$$

where $f(x_i)$ is the mean titre on day $x_i$ and $\sigma$ is the standard deviation of the
titres around the curve, the same on every day ($\sigma^2$ is the variance of the model).
The mean of a Normal distribution can take any real value, so the curve needs no outer
function to give it the right range (see
[From a response curve to a model for observations](../Theory.qmd#sec-response-observation)).
The units of $a$ and $b$ are those of Chapter 5: $b$ is in 1/day, because $bx$ is the
argument of an exponential and has no units, and $a$ is in units of titre/day, because $ax$
must have the units of the titre. The standard deviation $\sigma$ measures the spread of
the observations, so it has the units of the titre (log10 infectious doses).

A Normal model gives a positive probability to negative titres, which do not occur in these
data. This does not matter when that probability is negligible. The titres lie between 4.2
and 8.5 and vary by about one unit among the observations of the same day, so if the curve
passes near the observations its value lies many standard deviations above zero. We check
this after the fit.

### Question 2

The NLL has the form of the theory: a list of parameters, with the logarithms of the three
positive parameters, and a list of data, with the predictor (`day`) and the response
(`titre`). Because `day` is a vector, the line of the curve returns the mean titre of every
observation, and `dnorm()` uses the mean of each observation:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of the Ricker curve with a Normal observation model.
normal_nll = function(parms, data) {
  # Make the elements of both lists available by name.
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Transform the parameters to the original scale.
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma)
  # Mean titre on the day of each observation.
  mu = a * day * exp(-b * day)
  -sum(dnorm(x = titre, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}
```

We start from the values read by eye in Chapter 5. For $\sigma$ we take 1 unit of titre,
roughly the spread of the observations of one day. We give the starting values to
`MakeADFun()` on the log scale and fit the model:

```{r}
# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

# Starting values: the values read by eye in the Chapter 5 practical, and sigma = 1.
titre_start = list(log_a = log(3.44), log_b = log(1 / 6), log_sigma = log(1))

# Process the NLL, minimise it with BFGS and check the convergence code.
normal_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(normal_nll, titre_data), titre_start, silent = TRUE)
normal_fit = optim(
  par = normal_obj$par,
  fn = normal_obj$fn,
  gr = normal_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
normal_fit$convergence

# Estimates on the original scale.
a_mle = exp(normal_fit$par[["log_a"]])
b_mle = exp(normal_fit$par[["log_b"]])
sigma_mle = exp(normal_fit$par[["log_sigma"]])
c(a = a_mle, b = b_mle, sigma = sigma_mle)
```

The convergence code is 0. The estimates are $\hat a\approx3.42$ units of titre/day,
$\hat b\approx0.165$/day and $\hat\sigma\approx0.67$ units of titre. The first two are
close to the values read by eye (3.44 and 0.167). We can now check the argument of
question 1. The lowest mean titre in the data is the one of day 2, and the probability
that the fitted model gives to a negative titre on that day is the cumulative probability
of zero:

```{r}
# Ricker function: initial slope a and rate b.
ricker = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x * exp(-b * x)
}

# Mean titre on day 2 under the fitted model, and the probability of a negative titre.
ricker(2, a = a_mle, b = b_mle)
pnorm(q = 0, mean = ricker(2, a = a_mle, b = b_mle), sd = sigma_mle)
```

The mean titre on day 2 is 4.9, more than seven standard deviations above zero, and the
probability of a negative titre is of the order of $10^{-13}$. The Normal model can be used
here because the titres are far from zero compared with their spread.

We draw the fitted curve over the data, together with the curve by eye of Chapter 5
(@fig-titre_fit):

```{r}
#| label: fig-titre_fit
#| fig-cap: "Titre of the myxoma virus of grade 1 against the time since infection, with the Ricker curve fitted by maximum likelihood under a Normal model (solid line) and the curve read by eye in Chapter 5 (dashed line)."
# Observations, with axes that start at zero.
plot(titre ~ day, data = titre_data, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10),
     xlab = "Time since infection (days)", ylab = "Virus titre (log10 infectious doses)")

# Fitted curve and curve by eye.
curve(ricker(x, a = a_mle, b = b_mle), add = TRUE, col = "#D55E00")
curve(ricker(x, a = 3.44, b = 1 / 6), add = TRUE, lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Maximum likelihood", "By eye (Chapter 5)"),
       lty = c(1, 2), col = c("#D55E00", "black"), bty = "n")
```

The two curves are almost the same. The peak that we read by eye happened to be close to
the peak of the fitted curve, and in the Ricker function the peak determines both
parameters.

### Question 3

The time and the height of the peak are quantities calculated from the parameters, so we
ask for their standard errors with `ADREPORT()` inside the NLL, as in
[Uncertainty of the fitted curve](../Theory.qmd#sec-delta-method). We also mark the titres
with `OBS()`, which question 4 needs in order to simulate. We process the new NLL and fit
it again (the estimates do not change):

```{r}
# The NLL with the time and the height of the peak in ADREPORT(), and the titres marked
# as observations for the simulations of question 4.
normal_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  titre = OBS(titre)
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma)
  # Time (days) and height (units of titre) of the peak of the curve.
  peak_time = 1 / b
  peak_titre = a / (b * exp(1))
  ADREPORT(peak_time)
  ADREPORT(peak_titre)
  mu = a * day * exp(-b * day)
  -sum(dnorm(x = titre, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL and fit it again.
normal_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(normal_nll, titre_data), titre_start, silent = TRUE)
normal_fit = optim(
  par = normal_obj$par,
  fn = normal_obj$fn,
  gr = normal_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
normal_fit$convergence
```

`summary()` of the result of `sdreport()` has one row for each parameter, on the scale
that was optimised, and one row for each quantity in `ADREPORT()`, on the scale on which
it was calculated. `cov2cor()` gives the correlations between the estimates of the
parameters:

```{r}
# Standard errors of the parameters (log scale) and of the two quantities of the peak.
normal_sd = sdreport(normal_obj)
summary(normal_sd)
cov2cor(normal_sd$cov.fixed)
```

The standard errors on the log scale are about 0.06 for $\log(\hat a)$ and $\log(\hat b)$,
so both parameters are estimated to within a few percent, and 0.14 for
$\log(\hat\sigma)$. The estimates of $\log(a)$ and $\log(b)$ are strongly correlated
(0.95): a curve with a steeper initial rise (a larger $a$) must also decline sooner (a
larger $b$) to keep its peak at the height of the observations.

We asked for the time and the height of the peak on their original scale, in days and in
units of titre, so their Wald intervals are calculated on that scale. The theory calculates
Wald intervals on a scale on which the quantity is unbounded
([Uncertainty of the fitted curve](../Theory.qmd#sec-delta-method)), because an interval on
the original scale can cross the bound when the estimate is close to it. Both quantities
are positive, but their estimates lie about 16 and 50 standard errors above zero, so here
an interval on the original scale cannot reach the bound:

```{r}
# 95% Wald intervals of the time and the height of the peak, on the original scale.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
peak_summary = summary(normal_sd, select = "report")
cbind(
  estimate = peak_summary[, "Estimate"],
  lower = peak_summary[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * peak_summary[, "Std. Error"],
  upper = peak_summary[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * peak_summary[, "Std. Error"]
)
```

The peak is estimated on day 6.05 (95% Wald interval from 5.30 to 6.80 days) at a titre of
7.61 (from 7.32 to 7.91). The height is well determined because many observations lie near
the peak.

For the likelihood profile interval we profile $\log(b)$, transform the endpoints back
with `exp()`, and obtain the interval for the time of the peak from that of $b$. The
function $1/b$ decreases as $b$ increases, so the endpoints swap:

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Profile of log(b). The profile contains the estimate twice, so confint() warns that it
# collapses repeated values; the warning can be ignored.
normal_profile_b = TMB::tmbprofile(normal_obj, name = "log_b", trace = FALSE)

# 95% interval for b (1/day), and for the time of the peak (days).
b_interval = exp(confint(normal_profile_b))
b_interval
rev(1 / b_interval)
```

The likelihood profile interval of $b$ goes from 0.144/day to 0.186/day, almost
symmetrically around the estimate of 0.165. The corresponding interval for the time of the
peak goes from 5.36 to 6.95 days: it extends 0.69 days below the estimate and 0.89 days
above it, because $1/b$ is a curve that stretches the values of $b$ below the estimate more
than those above it. The Wald interval for the time of the peak (5.30 to 6.80 days) is
symmetric by construction, because the delta method treats $1/b$ as a straight line near
the estimate. So, compared with the profile interval, it is shifted towards earlier days.
The two intervals differ by less than a fifth of a day at each end, which is small compared
with their width; the extra Exercise 4 shows what it means for the coverage of the Wald
interval.

### Question 4

The titres are marked with `OBS()`, so the function `simulate()` of the object draws one
hypothetical sample of 27 titres, on the same days as the data, for the parameter values
that we give it. We store 1,000 hypothetical samples in a matrix with one row per
observation:

```{r}
# 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 27 titres at the estimates: one row per observation
# and one column per hypothetical sample.
n_sim = 1000
normal_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = length(titre_data$titre), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 611)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  normal_simulations[, j] = normal_obj$simulate(normal_fit$par)$titre
}
```

`DHARMa::createDHARMa()` calculates the residuals from the simulations, with the arguments
of the [theory](../Theory.qmd#sec-response-residuals). The expected value of each
observation is the mean titre of its day, and the titres are continuous, so
`integerResponse = FALSE`: two titres are almost never equal, and no ties need to be drawn
at random. `plot()` draws the two standard panels (@fig-titre_residuals), and
`DHARMa::plotResiduals()` with the argument `form` draws the residuals against the day
(@fig-titre_residuals_day):

```{r}
#| label: fig-titre_residuals
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of the Normal model with the Ricker curve, from 1,000 hypothetical samples. Left: quantile–quantile plot against a uniform distribution. Right: residuals against the rank of the expected titre."
# Expected titre of each observation under the fitted model.
normal_expected = ricker(titre_data$day, a = a_mle, b = b_mle)

# Scaled quantile residuals from the simulations, and the two standard panels.
normal_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = normal_simulations,
  observedResponse = titre_data$titre,
  fittedPredictedResponse = normal_expected,
  integerResponse = FALSE
)
plot(normal_residuals)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-titre_residuals_day
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of the Normal model with the Ricker curve against the day of the observation."
# Residuals against the day of the observation.
DHARMa::plotResiduals(normal_residuals, form = titre_data$day)
```

In the quantile–quantile plot the residuals follow the line, so their distribution is
close to uniform, and none lies outside the range of its simulations. The right panel of
@fig-titre_residuals orders the observations by their expected titre, which first increases
and then decreases with the day, so the pattern in time is clearer in
@fig-titre_residuals_day. There the residuals tend to lie above 0.5 on the first days and
on the last days, and below 0.5 around the peak: the observations lie slightly above the
curve at both ends and slightly below it in the middle. This agrees with what we saw by eye
in Chapter 5: the titre levels off after day 6, while the Ricker curve must decline after
its peak. In @fig-titre_residuals_day DHARMa draws the line of the upper quartile in red,
because its test gives a small p-value. As in the theory, we read the plot as exploratory
evidence and not as a decision: with 27 observations and one to six per day the pattern
rests on few observations, but it suggests that the Ricker curve describes the titre after
the peak only approximately. A curve with a third parameter, such as the
[generalised Ricker](../../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-generalised-ricker)
function, could be fitted and compared with it.

DHARMa also calculates a dispersion statistic, but for a Normal model it is not informative:
$\sigma$ is estimated from the spread of the observations around the curve, so the
simulated spread matches the observed spread almost by construction.

### Question 5

A Gamma distribution with shape $k$ and scale $\mu/k$ has mean $\mu$ and variance
$k(\mu/k)^2=\mu^2/k$, so its standard deviation is $\mu/\sqrt{k}$: the spread of the titres
is proportional to the mean, with a coefficient of variation $1/\sqrt{k}$ that is the same
on every day. In the Normal model the spread is the same on every day, whatever the mean.
The Gamma model also gives a probability of zero to negative titres. The NLL takes the
logarithm of the shape as its third parameter; we start from the values by eye and a shape
of 10:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of the Ricker curve with a Gamma observation model.
gamma_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  shape = exp(log_shape)
  mu = a * day * exp(-b * day)
  # A scale of mu / shape gives each observation the mean mu.
  -sum(dgamma(x = titre, shape = shape, scale = mu / shape, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the NLL and fit it.
gamma_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(gamma_nll, titre_data),
  list(log_a = log(3.44), log_b = log(1 / 6), log_shape = log(10)),
  silent = TRUE
)
gamma_fit = optim(
  par = gamma_obj$par,
  fn = gamma_obj$fn,
  gr = gamma_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
gamma_fit$convergence

# Estimates on the original scale.
c(a = exp(gamma_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = exp(gamma_fit$par[["log_b"]]),
  shape = exp(gamma_fit$par[["log_shape"]]))
```

The fit converged, with $\hat a\approx3.56$ units of titre/day, $\hat b\approx0.171$/day
and a shape of about 90, which gives a coefficient of variation of about 0.11 (a standard
deviation of about 0.8 units of titre at the peak and 0.5 on day 2). Both models have
three parameters and are fitted to the same 27 titres in the same units, so we can compare
them with the criteria of the theory, with $n=27$:

```{r}
# AIC, AICc and BIC of the two models, with K = 3 parameters and n = 27 observations.
n_obs = length(titre_data$titre)
k_models = c(normal = 3, gamma = 3)
nll_models = c(normal = normal_fit$value, gamma = gamma_fit$value)
aic = 2 * k_models + 2 * nll_models
aicc = aic + 2 * k_models * (k_models + 1) / (n_obs - k_models - 1)
bic = k_models * log(n_obs) + 2 * nll_models
rbind(aic = aic, aicc = aicc, bic = bic)
```

All three criteria prefer the Normal model, by 4.0 units. The difference is the same for
the three criteria because the two models have the same number of parameters and are
fitted to the same observations: the penalty is the same for both models within each
criterion, and the difference between the models is twice the difference between their
maximum log-likelihoods. So the comparison says that the titres are more probable under a
spread that is the same on every day than under a spread that grows with the mean. This is
plausible, because the titre is already a logarithm: variation by a constant factor in the
number of infectious doses becomes a constant spread on the logarithmic scale. With 27
observations, however, the evidence is moderate. The curve itself hardly depends on the
choice: the estimates of $a$ and $b$ differ by a few percent between the two models.

# Exercise 2: Enzyme kinetics

The data set `Puromycin` of base R contains the rate of an enzymatic reaction (`rate`, in
counts/min/min) at six concentrations of the substrate (`conc`, in parts per million,
ppm), measured in cells that were treated with the antibiotic puromycin (12 observations)
and in untreated cells (11 observations) (Treloar 1974, in Bates and Watts 1988). The
column `state` says to which of the two groups an observation belongs. Load the data with
`data(Puromycin, package = "datasets")`.

In Exercise 6 of the Chapter 5 practical we placed a
[Michaelis–Menten](../../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-michaelis-menten)
curve, $f(x)=ax/(b+x)$, by eye over the observations of each state: $a=210$ counts/min/min
for the treated cells and $a=165$ counts/min/min for the untreated cells, with $b=0.06$
ppm for both. By eye, the states differed in the asymptote and not in the half-maximum. In
this exercise we fit and compare two models with a Normal observation model with a constant
standard deviation $\sigma$, and treat the 23 observations as independent.

1. Write the model with one Michaelis–Menten curve for both states, with the units of $a$,
   $b$ and $\sigma$. Fit it, starting from values close to those read by eye, check the
   convergence, and draw the curve over the data with a different symbol for each state.
   Hint: the list of data holds the predictor and the response, as in
   [Fitting a response curve by maximum likelihood](../Theory.qmd#sec-fit-response). In
   `plot()`, the argument `pch = ifelse(Puromycin$state == "treated", 16, 1)` draws the
   treated cells as filled circles and the untreated cells as open circles.
2. Fit a model in which each state has its own asymptote $a$, with a common $b$ and
   $\sigma$. Use an index vector with the number of the state of each observation, as in
   question 6 of Exercise 1 of the
   [Chapter 4 practical](../../Chapter_4/Practicals/no_solution.qmd). Draw both curves
   over the data. How does the estimate of $\sigma$ change, and why? Hint: `as.numeric()`
   of the factor `state` gives the index vector. If `log_a` starts as a vector of two
   values, `a[state]` inside the NLL is the asymptote of each observation, and the first
   two elements of the `par` of the fit are the two values of `log_a`.
3. Ask for the difference between the two asymptotes with `ADREPORT()`, and calculate a 95%
   Wald interval for it. On which scale do you calculate the interval, and why? What does
   the treatment with puromycin do to the maximum rate of the reaction? Hint: the
   difference is calculated inside the NLL, as the difference between two probabilities in
   that question of the Chapter 4 practical; for the scale, see
   [Uncertainty of the fitted curve](../Theory.qmd#sec-delta-method).
4. Calculate the likelihood profile interval of $b$ in the model of question 2 and compare
   it with the Wald interval from the log scale. Why do the two intervals agree so much
   better than those for the handling time of the reed frogs in the theory? Hint: compare
   the range of the concentrations with the estimated half-maximum, and recall where the
   densities of the reed frog tanks stopped ("Standard errors and correlation of the
   parameters" and "Likelihood profile intervals of the parameters" in
   [Uncertainty of a response curve](../Theory.qmd#sec-curve-uncertainty)).
5. Compare the two models with AIC, AICc and BIC. Do the criteria agree? Hint: see
   "Information criteria" in [Comparing candidate models](../Theory.qmd#sec-response-comparison).
6. Simulate 1,000 hypothetical samples from the model that the criteria prefer, calculate
   the scaled quantile residuals with DHARMa, and plot them, also against the concentration
   of the substrate. What do you see, and what can you conclude from 23 observations? Hint:
   proceed as in question 4 of Exercise 1 (the rates must be marked with `OBS()` in the
   NLL); the expected rate of an observation is the curve of its state at its
   concentration.

# Exercise 3: Fecundity of fir trees

The data set `FirDBHFec_sum` in the package `emdbook` contains the diameter at breast
height (`DBH`, in cm) and the fecundity (`fecundity`) of 333 balsam fir trees (*Abies
balsamea*) on Whiteface Mountain, New York (Silvertown and Dodd 1999; Dodd and Silvertown
2000). Fecundity was measured as the number of cone rachises on a tree: the rachis is the
axis of a cone, which stays on the branch after the cone has fallen apart. Load the data
with `data(FirDBHFec_sum, package = "emdbook")`.

In Exercise 7 of the Chapter 5 practical we described the mean fecundity with a
[power law](../../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-power),
$\mu(x)=ax^b$, where $x$ is the diameter, and read $a=0.5$ and $b=2$ from two points of the
cloud. The trees come from two populations (the column `pop`). We do not model this
grouping: we treat the trees as independent observations of one curve, which is a
simplification ([Chapter 7](../../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd) deals with observations that come
in groups).

1. As in Exercise 7 of the Chapter 5 practical, remove the trees with a missing diameter,
   and check that no fecundity is missing. Why can a missing value not be replaced by
   zero? Some fecundities are not whole numbers: find them and decide what to do with them
   before you fit a model for counts. Hint: `x != round(x)` is `TRUE` for the elements of
   `x` that are not whole numbers. Rounding them and removing those trees are both
   defensible; say which you choose and why.
2. Write a [Poisson](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-poisson) model whose mean
   follows the power law, with the units of $a$. Fit it from the values read by eye in
   the Chapter 5 practical, and check it with scaled quantile residuals from DHARMa and the
   dispersion statistic. Hint: the mean must be positive, but the exponent $b$ can take any
   real value, so only $a$ needs a transformation (see
   [From a response curve to a model for observations](../Theory.qmd#sec-response-observation)).
   For the residuals, follow
   [Checking the fitted model](../Theory.qmd#sec-response-residuals): the counts are whole
   numbers, as the numbers killed of the reed frogs were.
3. Fit a [Negative Binomial](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-negative_binomial)
   model with the same curve, with `dnbinom2()` of RTMBdist (mean and shape $k$). Check its
   residuals, and draw the curves of both models over the data. Hint: `dnbinom2()` takes
   the mean in `mu` and the shape, which is positive, in `size`.
4. Compare the two models with AIC, AICc and BIC. Hint: $n$ is the number of trees (see
   "Information criteria" in [Comparing candidate models](../Theory.qmd#sec-response-comparison)).
5. For the model that the criteria prefer, calculate the likelihood profile interval of the
   exponent $b$, and from it an interval for the factor $2^b$ by which the mean fecundity
   changes when the diameter doubles. Do the data support a fecundity proportional to the
   cross-sectional area of the trunk ($b=2$)? Hint: see "Likelihood profile intervals of
   the parameters" in [Uncertainty of a response curve](../Theory.qmd#sec-curve-uncertainty)
   for transforming the endpoints of an interval; $2^b$ increases with $b$.
6. For the same model, calculate the mean fecundity on a grid of diameters from 3 to 18 cm
   with `ADREPORT()`, and its pointwise 95% confidence band from Wald intervals on the log
   scale. Draw the curve and its band over the data. Where along the diameters is the
   curve best determined, and why? Hint: follow
   [Uncertainty of the fitted curve](../Theory.qmd#sec-delta-method), with the logarithm of
   the mean in place of the logit of the probability; `lines()` adds the curve and the two
   limits of the band to the plot.

# Exercise 4: Coverage of an interval for the time of the peak

This exercise is extra practice. In Exercise 1 the Wald interval and the likelihood profile
interval for the time of the peak differed, and from one sample we cannot tell how often
either of them contains the time of the peak of the data generating process. As in
Exercise 5 of the [Chapter 4 practical](../../Chapter_4/Practicals/no_solution.qmd), we
can find out by simulating hypothetical samples from a model whose parameters we know:
here the Normal model fitted in Exercise 1, with the estimates as its parameters (see
"Coverage checked by simulation" in
[Chapter 4](../../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-uncertainty)). This exercise
continues with the objects of Exercise 1. The function that runs the simulation is given
below the questions with two gaps, which you fill in.

1. Complete the first gap of the function `simulate_peak_time()` below. Set seed 641 and
   simulate 2,000 hypothetical samples of the 27 titres, on the same days, from the fitted
   Normal model. Each sample is fitted from the values read by eye, as the data were. How
   many fits failed? Calculate the bias of the estimator of the time of the peak, with its
   Monte Carlo standard error, and compare the standard deviation of the estimates with
   the standard error of Exercise 1. Hint: the list of data of each sample needs the names
   that `normal_nll()` uses, `day` and `titre`. The bias is the mean of the estimates minus
   the time of the peak used to simulate, $1/\hat b$ of Exercise 1. A **Monte Carlo standard
   error** measures how much a result of the simulation would vary if it were repeated with
   other random samples; for the bias, a mean of 2,000 estimates, it is the standard
   deviation of the estimates divided by $\sqrt{2000}$.
2. Complete the second gap, which calculates the 95% Wald interval for the time of the
   peak from the row of `ADREPORT()`, and calculate the coverage of the interval with its
   Monte Carlo standard error. (The coverage of the likelihood profile interval would need
   `tmbprofile()` in every sample, which takes much longer, so we do not simulate it
   here.) Hint: the coverage is a proportion $c$ of 2,000 samples, so its Monte Carlo
   standard error is $\sqrt{c(1-c)/2000}$, as in the solution of Exercise 5 of the
   [Chapter 4 practical](../../Chapter_4/Practicals/solution.qmd).
3. In how many samples does the interval lie entirely below the time of the peak that was
   used to simulate, and in how many entirely above it? What does this suggest, given the
   two intervals of question 3 of Exercise 1?
4. Why do these results only approximate the behaviour of the interval for the real
   rabbits?

The function below needs `normal_nll()`, `normal_obj`, `normal_fit`, `titre_data` and
`titre_start` from Exercise 1, the helper `cmb()`, and the object `critical_value` (the
critical value of the standard Normal distribution for a 95% interval). It draws every
sample with the function `simulate()` of the fitted object, and stores the results of
every sample in one row of a data frame. In each gap, replace `NA` by your own code. The
lines that follow a gap use the names of the objects that the gap creates, so keep those
names.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Hypothetical samples of the 27 titres from the Normal model fitted in Exercise 1. For
# each sample: the estimate of the time of the peak, its 95% Wald interval, and whether
# the fit converged.
simulate_peak_time = function(n_samples) {
  results = data.frame(
    estimate = rep(NA, times = n_samples),
    lower = rep(NA, times = n_samples),
    upper = rep(NA, times = n_samples),
    converged = rep(NA, times = n_samples)
  )
  for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
    # One hypothetical sample: titres on the same days, simulated at the estimates.
    titre_sim = normal_obj$simulate(normal_fit$par)$titre

    # GAP 1: connect normal_nll() to the days and the simulated titres and process it
    # with MakeADFun(), starting from titre_start, and store the result in an object
    # called sim_obj. Then fit it with optim() and method = "BFGS", and store the result
    # in an object called sim_fit.
    sim_obj = NA
    sim_fit = NA

    # GAP 2: from the row peak_time of summary(sdreport(sim_obj), select = "report"),
    # the estimate of the time of the peak and the endpoints of its 95% Wald interval on
    # the original scale, in objects called estimate, lower and upper.
    estimate = NA
    lower = NA
    upper = NA

    results$estimate[i] = estimate
    results$lower[i] = lower
    results$upper[i] = upper
    results$converged[i] = sim_fit$convergence == 0
  }
  results
}
```
